written: 2026-11-20, after SeedLM-15, before any tie rule other than the order was scored
motivation: With the same thirteen coders, only the order in which tied behaviours are compared moved the vote between 68 and 76 held-out teacher tasks (SeedLM-15): ties are frequent and decide several tasks
hypothesis: Breaking ties by simplicity (the tied behaviour whose shortest program has the fewest tokens) beats breaking them by a random order
method: scripts/seedlm16_occam.py over SeedLM-15's cached proposals: SeedLM-10's vote; among proposals with the highest support, the one with the fewest pyx tokens; remaining ties by the subset's random order. 200 random subsets per size, the same seeds as SeedLM-15's scoring
primary_measure: held-out teacher tasks, 13 coders: the mean over 200 orders with the simplicity tie-break against SeedLM-15's 71.03. Supported if at least 1.5 higher; not supported if lower; inconclusive otherwise
secondary_measures: the whole curve on held-out teacher tasks and the development fifth
the spread over orders at 13 coders (SeedLM-15: sd 1.48 on teacher tasks)
choice: diagnostic only; no method is adopted from it

outcome.primary: held-out teacher tasks, 13 coders: 72.86 with the simplicity tie-break (sd 0.35 over 200 orders, 72 to 73) against 71.03 (sd 1.48): +1.8, supported (reports/seedlm/ensemble_occam.json)
outcome.reading: On generated tasks the simplest of the equally supported behaviours is right more often, and the vote no longer depends on the order of the coders. On real development tasks simplicity does not help: there the shorter program is often the engine-like coincidence
